title: The Embarrassingly Parallel Problem: When Students Understand the Parts But Not The Whole
author: Carl Hendrick
source: The Learning Dispatch on Substack, February 7, 2026
summary: Hendrick borrows a computer science concept—the 'embarrassingly parallel problem'—to expose a fundamental mismatch in educational technology. Parallel processing breaks tasks into independent sub-components that can be executed simultaneously with zero coordination; serial processing requires sequential execution where one output becomes the next task's input. Learning science has identified robust mechanisms (spacing, retrieval practice, interleaving, feedback) that operate in parallel and scale beautifully via technology. But deep understanding is emphatically serial: it requires sequencing, connection, and integration that no algorithm can replicate. The result is a troubling pattern in meta-analyses: effect sizes on curriculum-aligned tests are 2-3 times larger than on standardized tests—a signal that students acquire isolated components but fail to assemble them into flexible, transferable knowledge. Hendrick shows how platforms like ALEKS fail when deployed as substitutes for teacher instruction (effect size = 0.05) but succeed when supplementing human-led teaching (0.43)—the teacher provides the serial layer of sequencing and contextualizing that the platform cannot. The atomization trap is real: students can pass skill checks but cannot write arguments, solve reframed problems, or explain why facts matter. The answer is not to abandon technology but to respect the distinction: exploit the parallel infrastructure for diagnosis, practice, and feedback while zealously protecting the teacher's irreducible work of building coherent understanding through sequencing, connection, and judgment.
points: Much of learning science works on parallel processes (spacing, retrieval practice, interleaving, immediate feedback) that scale beautifully via technology—but deep understanding is emphatically serial.
The 2-3 times larger effect sizes on curriculum-aligned tests versus standardized assessments reveal that students master isolated skills without assembling them into flexible knowledge.

Technology succeeds as a supplement to teacher-led instruction (providing the parallel layer of practice and feedback) but fails as a substitute (it cannot provide the serial work of sequencing and integration).
The atomization trap: students can retrieve isolated facts, pass skill checks, and apply practiced procedures—yet fail to apply knowledge in novel contexts or understand why it matters.

The best educational technology parallels what can be parallelized (routine practice, scheduling, diagnostics) while preserving and supporting what cannot: the teacher's capacity to sequence ideas, connect components, and build coherent understanding.
quotes: the central conundrum in instructional design is this: firstly, how to disassemble a domain of knowledge into teachable parts without destroying what made it a domain in the first place.

The decomposition of knowledge is necessary because novices cannot apprehend the whole all at once; working memory will not permit it. But the reassembly is where instruction most reliably fails, because the connections between components are not themselves components.
Learning, at its most meaningful, is emphatically not embarrassingly parallel.
The parallel layer is working. The serial layer is not being adequately served.

An example of this I am fond of using is from a study by George Miller and Patricia Gildea... One child, having learned that 'correlate' means 'be related,' wrote: 'Me and my parents correlate, because without them I wouldn't be here.
This is the atomisation trap in miniature: every component mastered, but no guarantee they recombine into understanding.
The parallel layer is not standing still; it is getting substantially more sophisticated.

What curriculum-aligned tests measure is whether the parallel processes worked; what standardised tests measure, however imperfectly, is whether those acquisitions have been integrated into something more flexible.” Archived from The Learning Dispatch on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
